questions.q: What is a jailbreak, as defined in this lesson?
options: A software exploit that modifies a model's trained weights directly
An input crafted to circumvent a model's safety training and elicit a disallowed output
A type of reward model used in RLAIF
A formal proof that a model is misaligned
questions.explain: A jailbreak is a crafted prompt or sequence of prompts designed to get a model to produce output its safety training was meant to prevent — not a modification of the model itself.

questions.q: Why can jailbreaks work at all against a model that has gone through safety training?
options: Because safety training is never actually applied to deployed models
Because safety training covers a finite sample of phrasings, while the space of possible inputs is effectively unbounded, creating a distributional gap
Because refusal behavior is chosen at random for each request
Because all models are trained identically regardless of lab
questions.explain: The distributional gap is the mismatch between what safety training sampled and the much larger space of ways a request could be phrased. Reliability degrades as phrasing drifts from the training distribution.

questions.q: Conceptually, what does roleplay or persona framing exploit, according to this lesson?
options: A flaw in the model's underlying mathematical architecture
The gap between a request's underlying intent and how it pattern-matches against what refusal training learned to recognize as a direct harmful request
A bug that only affects models trained before 2020
The model's inability to process any fictional content whatsoever
questions.explain: Wrapping a request in a fictional or hypothetical frame can leave the underlying ask functionally unchanged while shifting how it matches the patterns refusal training recognized.

questions.q: What does documented research on many-shot context stuffing show?
options: Long contexts have no measurable effect on model behavior
Very long adversarial contexts can measurably erode refusal behavior that holds reliably at shorter context lengths
It only works on models with no safety training at all
It is identical in mechanism to obfuscation and encoding
questions.explain: Research on many-shot jailbreaking has documented that a long run of context can shift a model's behavior pattern before the real request appears, weakening refusal behavior that holds at shorter lengths.

questions.q: According to this lesson, does patching a documented jailbreak pattern permanently close the distributional gap?
options: Yes — once a pattern is patched, no future jailbreak of any kind is possible
No — patching a known pattern narrows one instance of the gap, but the gap itself persists because the space of possible phrasings is effectively unbounded
Yes — because the distributional gap only ever contains a fixed, finite number of patterns
No — because labs never actually retrain models after discovering a jailbreak
questions.explain: The lesson frames this as an ongoing adversarial dynamic: defenders patch documented patterns (feeding back from red-teaming), but the underlying gap between finite training coverage and the unbounded space of inputs remains.
